title: Drawdown-Aware Sizing: How Should a Bot Earn Back Full Size Trading? (and the trap)
author: DesertClimber
selftext:
Sizing question for review and opinions.  :)

This bot runs both in a lab with variants, and on live accounts- This was a test on scaled sizing risks. Elevated risk was only initiated last week, Wed Sept 9th, while the strategy has been running for much longer, overall.  
  
The strategy is sized as a fixed percentage of the overall account balance, and runs concurrently on two live accounts. After a near two-day drawdown, the auto-sizing scaled back the position to avoid continued losses at elevated sizing. When this happened, both went into shadow mode and continue to record trades, no longer touching real money. After the drawdown slowed, I re-armed only one account, while the other stays in shadow- as a control, with the original rules. The live account is once again trading, but with tightened rules as a test.

The bot has a real but thin edge. 48%-51% win rate, with growth coming from win/loss asymmetry. A look at the account chart shows the two-day drawdown off the high around 09/16 around midnight. Note: The divergence seen in equity curves is normal, as other modules continue to run on the same account. This discussion is focused on 'SecretAgent' seen as the amber equity line. If the divergence grows to be too large, the bot may need to work off it's own cumulative PnL.  
  
The question: How should size come down in a losing run, and how does it come back without waiting a week? And, when should decelerating risk be used when account balance begins to grow?

This bot measures drawdown in 'units'- Each unit is the capital of a single full-size position at today's balance, so the brake is size-invariant: halving the base percentage doesn't mute it. From one unit below the module's own peak, size shrinks linearly; at five units it hits the floor, ¼ sizing. Four straight losses is about five units, and that's when it reaches the floor sizing.

Currently, the brake arrives at the floor at full-size speed and leaves it at quarter-size speed. Each win recovers a quarter of what a full-size loss took, so climbing back five units takes \~20 net wins. It's asymmetrical, hence getting trapped on/near the floor for long periods of time.

When the module is paused (placed into shadow) it's basically variance control, not edge correction since outcomes are independent from one trade to the next. A losing streak says nothing about the next trade- its expectancy is the same as any other. We tested "pause after N straight losses, resume on the first shadow win" for N = 3…6 on the replay: every version sat out trades that averaged positive. A pause lowers variance and forfeits expectancy. That's a legitimate trade-off if variance is what you can't afford; it is not a way to fix the edge. The edge is changed only by changing WHICH trades are taken, and the damage is bounded only by what's at risk when a bad day shows up.

Options for 'getting back up off the floor':  
  1. Streak pause. Stop after N losses, resume on the first shadow win. Forfeits positive expectancy on the replay for every N.  
  2. Rolling loss threshold. Pause when the last 40 trades net worse than \~3σ below expectancy; return next day at floor size. Fires \~2% of the time, after most of the damage.  
  3. Rolling peak. Floor ½ instead of ¼, full brake at 8 units instead of 5, and while pinned the peak reference decays toward current P&L by half a unit per trade taken without a loss. Full size back in \~10 non-losing trades; lost again just as fast. Variant: after X trades pinned, size steps up if the last Y shadow-scored signals are net positive.  
  4. Circuit breaker. Pinned and last 100 trades net negative → shadow. Return when the shadow rows' last 100 net positive. Slow both ways by design: catches "the edge is gone", not "the afternoon was bad".

NOTE:  
Disagreements between the two accounts cluster at regime changes, so the effective sample is the number of episodes.

The dollar drawdown is mostly sizing- Three of the last four losing sessions ran at six to seven times the size that earned the peak, while the per-trade edge over the full sample is intact.

Actual regime detection is unsolved. Nothing tested had day to day persistence. Every rule above is a variance rule; if regime truly has changed, only option 4 notices, and slowly.

comments.author: QSignalFX
comments.body:
Different horizon here (daily bars, equities, holds for weeks), so filter accordingly. I don't brake on drawdown at all: size is a fixed fraction, and the only thing that moves is which pools are allowed to open, gated by a daily regime read. That's your "edge only changes by changing which trades are taken" — I put all the effort there and none in sizing. On daily bars regime did have persistence for me, it's the strongest signal I have. Intraday, I believe you that it doesn't.

On the brake: you say a streak carries no information about the next trade. Then the asymmetry is pure cost — down at full speed, up at quarter speed is a bet that drawdowns mean something. Make it symmetric or drop it. And the line that jumps out is your last one: three of four losing sessions at 6–7× the size that made the peak. That's the size jump of the 9th, not the brake. You're asking the brake to fix a decision made upstream.
